wikipedia.title: Sprinkler (dance)
categories: Articles with unsourced statements from April 2025

profile.name: Sprinkler dance
profile.tagline: A novelty dance move mimicking a garden irrigation sprinkler.
profile.insight: In 2024, breakdancer Rachael Gunn brought the garden sprinkler to the Paris Olympics, decades after its 1980s Australian origins.
profile.profile: The Sprinkler dance is a novelty movement where a dancer places one hand on the back of their neck while waving the other arm and spinning to simulate an irrigation sprinkler. Originating in Australia during the 1980s, the dance gained renewed global fame when the England cricket team adopted it as a bonding exercise during the 2010–11 Ashes series. It subsequently exploded across the internet, featuring in films, television shows, and competitive breakdancing.
profile.profile_long: The Sprinkler dance operates as a kinetic imitation of mechanical garden machinery, requiring performers to mechanically cycle their upper bodies while rotating. Accounts of the dance's origins vary, with press coverage in December 2010 tracing its birth to Australia during the 1980s, alongside references to the disco era. The movement involves standing with legs slightly apart and knees slightly bent, bending the left elbow to place the left hand behind the head, and extending the right arm horizontally with a flat, vertical hand. The dancer rotates around the waist in a 180-degree sweep, pulling back three times before swinging the arm back across. Music and specific auditory accompaniments are not detailed in the sources, relying instead on the visual comedy and rhythm of the performer's body. The dance lacks traditional elaborate costumes, typically performed in casual athletic gear, team uniforms, or standard everyday clothing as seen in office spaces and schoolyards. Its primary cultural meaning shifted from a casual 1980s novelty to a potent symbol of team cohesion and viral internet culture. The movement found a home across popular culture, appearing in films such as House Party (1990) and A Night at the Roxbury (1998), television programs like Bluey (2018), and international sports arenas. Notable figures associated with its revival include cricketers Paul Collingwood and Graeme Swann of the England cricket team, as well as breakdancer Rachael Gunn during her 2024 Paris Olympics performance. Regional variants and strict lineages remain minimal, as the dance spread primarily through digital video diaries and social media broadcasting. Gaps in the historical record include any formal musical scores, indigenous roots, or standardized teaching syllabi.

sections.origins_and_history: Accounts of the dance's origins vary, with press coverage in December 2010 describing it as having originated in Australia during the 1980s alongside the era of The Bump. Its popularity saw a massive revival when the England cricket team adopted it during their winning 2010–11 Ashes series, turning it into an internet phenomenon.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Standing with legs slightly apart and knees slightly bent, the dancer bends their left elbow and places their left hand behind their head while outstretching the right arm inline with the shoulder. The dancer rotates around the waist in a 180-degree sweep, pulling back three times while moving the arm to the left before swinging it back to the right in one motion.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music and instruments are not described in the sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are not formally defined, with performers wearing athletic kits, cricket whites, or casual everyday clothing in settings ranging from indoor media rooms in Tasmania to ice rinks in Florida and the Melbourne Cricket Ground.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally used as a casual novelty, it was deployed by the England cricket team as a team bonding exercise during the Ashes series, later compared by captain Andrew Strauss to a personal version of the Māori haka.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include Paul Collingwood who introduced it to the England cricket team, Graeme Swann who documented it, and Rachael Gunn who performed it at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
sections.regional_variants: Regional variants are not documented, though the movement spread globally via the internet through fan clips, vicars, choirboys, and schoolchildren.
sections.lineage: The movement traces from 1980s Australian nightlife through to its 2010 viral revival by English cricketers and subsequent appearance in 21st-century media.

basic_steps: Stand with legs slightly apart and knees slightly bent
Bend left elbow and place left hand behind head
Outstretch right arm inline with right shoulder, hand flat in a vertical position
Rotate around the waist in a 180 degree sweep, pulling back three times while moving arm to the left
Swing right arm back to the right in one motion

gaps: Music genres, specific songs, and musical instruments are not mentioned in the sources.
Detailed historical documentation prior to the 1980s Australian origin account is thin.
